name: J. Herschel
description: A northern highland region near the lunar limb. Dominated by the ancient, heavily degraded J. Herschel crater (~165 km), one of the largest eroded impact structures in this zone. The southern margin touches the eastern extent of Mare Frigoris.

name: Plato
description: Features the iconic Plato crater (~101 km), a large walled plain whose floor is flooded with unusually dark mare basalt, making it one of the most visually distinctive craters on the near side. Located on the northern rim of Mare Imbrium, flanked by the Montes Alpes.

name: Aristoteles
description: Northern highland terrain between Mare Frigoris and Mare Serenitatis. Features Aristoteles crater (~87 km), a well-preserved impact structure with terraced walls and a hummocky floor. The paired presence of Aristoteles and Eudoxus makes this a visually prominent highland region.

name: Rumker
description: Features Mons Rümker, a large volcanic dome complex (~70 km across) rising from the basalt plains of northern Oceanus Procellarum. One of the most prominent volcanic constructs on the Moon — a cluster of coalesced lava domes rather than a single edifice. A scientifically important site for understanding lunar volcanism.

name: Sinus Iridium
description: 'Bay of Rainbows' — a large pre-Imbrian impact crater (~236 km) whose floor was completely flooded with mare basalt, leaving only the southern arc of its rim as the Montes Jura mountain range. The two prominent headlands, Cape Heraclides and Cape Laplace, frame the open bay where it meets Mare Imbrium. Note: LAC reference uses the spelling 'Sinus Iridum'; IAU-official spelling is 'Sinus Iridium'.

name: Cassini
description: Central northern region between Mare Imbrium and Mare Serenitatis. Features Cassini crater (~57 km), an ancient and heavily eroded walled plain containing two prominent interior craters — Cassini A and B — giving it a distinctive nested appearance. The eroded rim reflects great age.

name: Eudoxus
description: Northern highland terrain east of Mare Serenitatis. Features Eudoxus crater (~67 km), a relatively well-preserved impact structure with a central peak, flanked by the Montes Caucasus range to the west. Part of the heavily cratered highland zone separating the northern maria.

name: Geminus
description: Eastern highland region near the lunar limb. Features Geminus crater (~86 km), a well-preserved impact crater with a central peak and terraced inner walls, and the larger, more degraded Messala crater to the north. A classically cratered highland terrain.

name: Seleucus
description: Western Oceanus Procellarum — a broad expanse of basaltic mare plain. Features Seleucus crater (~43 km), a moderately fresh impact crater rising from the smooth mare surface. This region records some of the youngest basalt flows on the near side.

name: Aristarchus
description: One of the most volcanically active regions on the Moon. Features Aristarchus crater (~40 km), the brightest crater on the near side due to its fresh, high-reflectance ejecta. Adjacent Vallis Schröteri (Schröter's Valley) is the largest sinuous rille on the Moon, winding ~160 km from the Aristarchus Plateau — evidence of ancient lava tube collapse. Repeated transient lunar phenomena have been observed here.

name: Timocharis
description: Central Mare Imbrium — one of the smoothest mare plains on the near side. Features Timocharis crater (~34 km), a relatively fresh Copernican-age impact with a small ray system. The surrounding basalt plains of Mare Imbrium are among the most extensively studied regions in lunar geology.

name: Montes Apenninus
description: Features the Montes Apenninus, the highest mountain range on the Moon (~5 km above the surrounding mare), forming the southeastern rim of the Imbrium impact basin. Hadley Rille — a prominent sinuous rille — runs along the mountain front. Apollo 15 landed at Hadley-Apennine in July 1971, the first mission to use a lunar roving vehicle. Astronauts collected samples critical to understanding Imbrium basin geology.

name: Mare Serenitatis
description: 'Sea of Serenity' — a large, nearly circular mare basin (~700 km diameter) filled with dark basaltic lava flows of varying ages. Apollo 17 landed in the Taurus-Littrow valley on its southeastern margin in December 1972 — the last crewed lunar landing and the only mission to include a professional geologist (Harrison Schmitt). The mission returned the largest sample collection of any Apollo flight.

name: Macrobius
description: Eastern highland/mare boundary region at the western margin of Mare Crisium. Features Macrobius crater (~64 km), a moderately preserved impact structure. The region represents a transition between the ancient highland terrain and the younger basaltic plains of Mare Crisium.

name: Cleomedes
description: Northeastern highland region adjacent to Mare Crisium. Features Cleomedes crater (~126 km), a large, partially degraded walled plain with a flat floor and remnant central ridge. The region shows significant impact overlap characteristic of the ancient highland crust.

name: Hevelius
description: Western limb region where Oceanus Procellarum meets ancient highland terrain. Features Hevelius crater (~106 km), a large walled plain with a complex floor rille system (Rimae Hevelius). The overlapping craters Cavalerius and Lohrmann nearby reflect the heavily impacted history of this limb region.

name: Kepler
description: Central Oceanus Procellarum. Features Kepler crater (~32 km), a young Copernican-age impact crater with a prominent bright ray system extending hundreds of kilometers across the surrounding mare plains. The crater's fresh morphology — terraced walls, small central peak — makes it a textbook example of a well-preserved lunar impact.

name: Copernicus
description: Features Copernicus crater (~96 km), one of the most scientifically important and visually striking craters on the Moon. Its well-preserved terraced walls, multiple central peaks, and an extensive bright ray system — covering much of the central near side — make it the defining example of a complex impact crater. Approximately 800 million years old (Copernican Period), it defines a major time-stratigraphic boundary in lunar history. Bordered to the north by the Montes Carpatus.

name: Mare Vaporum
description: 'Sea of Vapors' — a relatively small mare (~245 km across) occupying the center of the near side. The region is geologically notable for Rima Hyginus, a linear rille featuring the collapse pit crater Hyginus, and nearby Rima Ariadaeus, one of the longest linear rilles on the Moon (~220 km). These features record ancient tectonic extension in the lunar crust.

name: Julius Caesar
description: Transition zone between the central highlands and the northern margin of Mare Tranquillitatis. Features Julius Caesar crater (~90 km), a heavily degraded ancient walled plain whose floor has been partially flooded by mare basalt. The region reflects the complex interplay between highland impact history and subsequent volcanic flooding.

name: Taruntius
description: Eastern mare region at the junction of Mare Fecunditatis and Mare Tranquillitatis. Features Taruntius crater (~56 km), a rare concentric crater with a well-defined interior ring — a morphology thought to reflect a shallow subsurface structure or unusual impact mechanics. Scientifically interesting as one of the clearest concentric craters on the near side.

name: Mare Undarum
description: 'Sea of Waves' — a small, irregular mare region east of Mare Crisium, partially flooded with basalt and heavily interpenetrated by highland terrain. One of the less prominent maria on the near side, representing incomplete flooding of a highland region.

name: Grimaldi
description: Western limb region featuring Grimaldi basin (~220 km), one of the oldest and darkest areas on the entire Moon. Its extremely low-reflectance basalt fill — among the darkest materials on the near side — makes it a prominent naked-eye dark spot. A pre-Nectarian impact basin, Grimaldi records some of the earliest lunar history. Nearby Riccioli crater shows similarly dark floor materials.

name: Letronne
description: Southern Oceanus Procellarum. Features Letronne crater (~116 km), a striking example of a mare-flooded impact structure whose northern wall has been almost completely submerged by lava flows, leaving a prominent open bay shape on the mare surface. The surviving southern arc of the rim stands in sharp contrast to the smooth surrounding plains.

name: Montes Riphaeus
description: Features the Montes Riphaeus (Riphaeus Mountains), a small isolated mountain range rising from the smooth basalt plains of Oceanus Procellarum. These mountains are remnants of ancient highland terrain that were not completely submerged by lava flooding — an island of pre-mare crust surrounded by volcanic plains. Note: LAC-76 official chart name is 'Montes Riphaeus'.

name: Ptolemaeus
description: Central near-side highlands featuring the magnificent Ptolemaeus–Alphonsus–Arzachel crater chain — three large overlapping craters showing a classic sequence of degradation. Ptolemaeus (~153 km) is the oldest and most eroded; Alphonsus (~118 km) features floor rilles and dark halo craters indicating volcanic outgassing; Arzachel (~97 km) is the youngest and most pristine with a prominent central peak. NASA's Ranger 9 spacecraft impacted in Alphonsus in March 1965, returning close-up photographs before impact.

name: Theophilus
description: Features the Theophilus–Cyrillus–Catharina trio at the western rim of Mare Nectaris — a textbook sequence illustrating progressive crater degradation. Theophilus (~100 km) is the youngest: sharp walls, prominent central peak complex, and terraced interior. Cyrillus is older and more eroded; Catharina is the most ancient and heavily degraded. Together they span hundreds of millions of years of impact history in a single field of view.

name: Colombo
description: Eastern highland/mare boundary region at the margin of Mare Fecunditatis. Features Colombo crater (~76 km), a moderately degraded walled plain. The region records the transition between the ancient highland crust and the basalt-filled 'Sea of Fertility' basin.

name: Langrenus
description: Features Langrenus crater (~132 km), one of the most visually impressive craters on the eastern near side. A well-preserved Eratosthenian-age impact with terraced inner walls, a central peak complex, and a relatively flat floor. Located on the eastern rim of Mare Fecunditatis, it is one of the first prominent features visible to the naked eye near the eastern limb.

name: Byrgius
description: Southwestern highland region near the lunar limb. Features Byrgius crater (~87 km), an ancient degraded walled plain. The small satellite crater Byrgius A, situated on the main crater's rim, is the source of a prominent bright ray system extending across the surrounding terrain — one of the most ray-intensive craters relative to its size on the near side.

name: Mare Humorum
description: 'Sea of Moisture' — a roughly circular mare basin (~389 km diameter) representing a well-defined ancient impact basin filled with basalt. The northern rim is marked by Gassendi crater (~110 km), a prominent flooded walled plain with an extraordinary network of floor rilles (Rimae Gassendi). Gassendi was seriously considered as an Apollo landing site due to its scientific complexity.

name: Pitatus
description: Southern highland/mare boundary. Features Pitatus crater (~97 km), a flooded walled plain at the southern edge of Mare Nubium whose floor is covered with a network of concentric and radial rilles (Rimae Pitatus). The partially submerged northern wall merges seamlessly with the mare surface — evidence of lava resurfacing after impact.

name: Purbach
description: Central southern highlands — a densely cratered ancient terrain. Features Purbach crater (~118 km) alongside Regiomontanus and Walter, three large overlapping pre-Nectarian walled plains recording the earliest period of intense lunar bombardment. The region exemplifies the heavily saturated highland crust.

name: Rupes Altai
description: Features the Rupes Altai (Altai Scarp), a sweeping curved escarpment approximately 480 km long and up to 3 km high — one of the most dramatic tectonic features on the near side. It represents an ancient fault scarp forming the inner ring of the Nectaris impact basin. Piccolomini crater (~88 km) sits prominently at the southern terminus of the scarp. The region provides a spectacular cross-section through basin ring tectonics.

name: Fracastorius
description: Features Fracastorius crater (~124 km) at the southern rim of Mare Nectaris — a classic mare-flooded impact structure. Its northern wall has been almost entirely erased by lava intrusion from the Nectaris basin, leaving a broad open arc that frames the southern shore of the 'Sea of Nectar'. The floor displays subtle wrinkle ridges indicative of lava subsidence.

name: Petavius
description: Features Petavius crater (~177 km), one of the largest and most complex impact craters on the near side. Its floor displays a prominent wide radial rille (Rima Petavius) extending from the central peak complex to the crater wall — one of the most striking floor rilles on the Moon. The central peaks rise ~3 km above the floor. A visually compelling and scientifically rich crater.

name: Schickard
description: Southwestern highland region featuring Schickard crater (~227 km), one of the largest impact craters on the near side. Its floor shows a geologically complex history of multiple lava flooding events of varying ages, visible as distinct zones of different albedo — lighter highland material, partially flooded patches, and darker mare basalt — making it an unusually well-exposed record of volcanic resurfacing.

name: Wilhelm
description: Southern highland region featuring Wilhelm crater (~106 km), a moderately degraded walled plain in a zone of ancient, heavily overlapping highland craters. Longomontanus crater to the west is a similarly well-preserved Nectarian-age structure. The region records dense impact saturation of the early lunar crust.

name: Tycho
description: Features Tycho crater (~85 km), one of the most prominent impact craters in the solar system. Its vast bright ray system extends across virtually the entire lunar near side — rays visible even to the naked eye during full Moon. A geologically young Copernican-age crater (~108 million years old), Tycho has a well-preserved morphology with terraced walls and a prominent central peak. Surveyor 7 landed just north of the rim in January 1968, returning the first close-up images of the southern highlands.

name: Maurolycus
description: One of the most densely cratered regions on the near side — a testament to the ancient, heavily bombarded highland crust. Maurolycus crater (~114 km) is partially overprinted by neighboring Barocius and the very large Stöfler crater (~126 km). This quadrangle offers one of the most dramatic illustrations of crater saturation and the cumulative record of early lunar bombardment.

name: Rheita
description: Southeastern highland region featuring Vallis Rheita, one of the longest crater chains on the Moon (~445 km). This striking linear feature is interpreted as a secondary impact chain formed by ejecta from the Nectaris basin impact event — a row of coalesced craters aligned radially from Nectaris. It provides direct evidence for basin-forming impact dynamics.

name: Schiller
description: Southwestern highland region featuring Schiller crater (~179 × 71 km), one of the most distinctively elongated large craters on the Moon. Its extreme length-to-width ratio suggests either a very low-angle oblique impact or the coalescence of two overlapping craters during the ancient bombardment period. The floor has been partially flooded with dark mare basalt, adding to its unusual appearance.

name: Clavius
description: Features Clavius crater (~225 km), one of the largest impact craters on the near side and among the largest on the Moon. Its floor displays a distinctive curved chain of progressively smaller craters — Rutherford, Porter, and several unnamed satellites — formed by later impacts. The sheer scale of Clavius makes it visible to the naked eye. It is also famous as the fictional site of a lunar base in Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey.

name: Hommel
description: Southern highland region approaching the lunar south pole, featuring heavily overlapping ancient impact craters in one of the most densely packed terrains on the near side. Hommel crater (~125 km) is substantially overprinted by Hommel C and other satellite impacts. The region — along with neighbors Pitiscus and Vlacq — represents some of the oldest exposed crust accessible on the near side.
